shared_text:
The flight. A wide-body airliner arriving in the afternoon at a high-elevation airport with higher terrain around it, which neither pilot had flown into before. Visual conditions, with thunderstorms along the route.

The crew. The captain was the pilot flying and the first officer the pilot monitoring. The crew had briefed the terrain at length before and during the flight, and for the approach.

What happened. About 200 miles out, the aircraft deviated around thunderstorms, and air traffic control changed the arrival and gave a crossing altitude of flight level 240. Approaching that fix, the crew were given a third arrival and told to expect a different runway. On that arrival they were sent direct to a fix, told to descend to 11,000 ft, and cleared for the instrument landing system approach. Passing the fix in vertical navigation path mode, the aircraft stayed at 11,000 ft instead of descending to 8,700 ft, as the crew expected for the next waypoint. This left the aircraft high on the glideslope. Approaching the final approach fix, the captain asked the first officer to request a left 360-degree turn to lose the excess height. Approach control approved it after confirming the aircraft was in visual conditions, which it was. About a quarter of the way round, the aircraft levelled at the final approach fix altitude of 7,700 ft. Because of the higher terrain in the area, the captain began a slow climb to about 8,200 ft for more clearance.
safe_outcome: The aircraft re-established on the final approach course, and the controller cleared it again for the approach and handed it to the tower. It never descended below 7,700 ft, there was no ground proximity warning, and it stayed in visual conditions throughout. The landing was uneventful. There was no conflict with other traffic. No one was hurt and the aircraft was not damaged.
bad_outcome: Another aircraft was descending nearby. Both crews received TCAS resolution advisories and followed them, and the aircraft passed about 300 feet vertically and half a mile apart. A flight attendant on this aircraft was thrown against a galley cart during the manoeuvre and received a minor injury.
bracket_fill: [climbing / descending / crossing] = descending; [this aircraft] = this aircraft
notes: Removed under rule 3: both 'Cause' and 'Suggestions' sections (three arrival changes and a late vector causing the high profile, the aircraft's reluctance to slow down, the turn being 'eye opening' and not something they would do in cloud, the alternatives of a steeper descent or a go-around, the wish for digital airport information), and 'out of the ordinary; hence this report'. Kept from those sections, as facts true at the time: the airport's high elevation, that neither pilot had been there before, and that the crew had briefed the terrain at length. Moved under rule 5: re-establishing on final, the new approach clearance, never descending below 7,700 ft, no ground proximity warning, remaining in visual conditions, and the landing. Removed under rule 6: the airport, runway numbers, arrival and fix names. Judgement calls: (1) the two narratives are near-identical copies, so they are treated as one account; (2) 'in the afternoon' comes from the coded local-time band; (3) 'the new clearance put us high on the glideslope' is rendered as 'this left the aircraft high on the glideslope'. Bracket: 'descending', because the aircraft turned a 360 and then climbed at the final approach fix, where the plausible conflict is following traffic descending on the same approach. No traffic interaction in the report, so the standard safe-ending sentences are used.
